sweep_summary: Navajo (nava1243, catalog TONAL on Sapir & Hoijer 1967 via SPA 1979). Four sweep items reduce to two works. (1) Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (Glottolog 167470) was located through the ANLA JSON API (record CA965L1976b) and fetched sources as an 86-page image-only scan (draft + typescript) from uafanlc.alaska.edu; three typescript pages were scanned at 300 dpi and the rest read from contact sheets. It is a comparative tonogenesis paper: PA vowel constriction and final glottalization become tone in the daughters, with Navajo showing constricted > low tone, non-constricted > high tone (pp.9, 11, 14). It never mentions stress or accent placement in Navajo: silent on the catalog coding, priority none. (2) McDonough 2003 'The prosody of interrogative and focus constructions in Navajo' appears three times in Glottolog (181704, 665186 dated 2002, and 673539 mis-authored to the editors Carnie et al.); all are the same Benjamins chapter, whose open author preprint was already on file. It is an intonation/focus study, but states first-hand that Navajo has a tone on every syllable, no metrical structure, and only default rightmost (verb-stem) phonetic prominence: confirms TONAL. No item contradicts or refines the catalog; no new deciding source found; nothing left to acquire from this sweep.alaska.edu host has a certificate-chain problem; curl -k was needed).

new_statements.quote: "McDonough (1990, 1996, 2000a, 2000b) has argued that metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo, and phenomena explained as metrical in Northern Athabaskan are the result of exclusively morphological imperatives in Navajo." ... "Instrumental studies indicate that the verb stem has many of the properties commonly associated to prominence: longer durations, pitch range expansion, semantic salience (McDonough and Ladefoged 1993, McDonough 1999). ... The stem is the only place in the word where the full set of phonemic contrasts occurs."

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the leading instrumental phonetician of Navajo: the language has a tone specified on every syllable and no metrical (stress) structure; the only word-level prominence is the phonetic salience of the word-final verb stem, which is a morphological, not a stress, effect. This agrees with the catalog's TONAL coding built on Sapir & Hoijer 1967 ('evenly stressed syllables, each bearing a tone'). This file was already held and cited as supporting evidence in the catalog record (fetched sources 2026-09-16); nothing read in this sweep is stronger. Leer 1976, the only genuinely new item, is a comparative tonogenesis paper and is silent on stress.

audit.reasoning: (1) Every quoted span in the record is present verbatim at the stated line locators in the held files (SPA 1979 djvu txt 335/344/374-378; McDonough & Willie txt 496-501; Iskarous txt 175-176; McDonough 2015 txt 124). The primary Sapir & Hoijer 1967 lines are second-hand via the SPA Handbook, which the record already flags. (2) The classification TONAL (H/L lexical tone on every syllable; word stress explicitly denied as 'evenly stressed syllables'; stem-final phonetic prominence hedged as stress-like) rests on the 1967 reference grammar plus McDonough's phonetic work. The best modern source, McDonough 2003 The Navajo Sound System, is not held, but McDonough's open 2003 Benjamins preprint fetched sources now states outright that 'metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo', that Navajo is 'a tone language with a tone specified for each syllable (Sapir-Hoijer 1967, Young and Morgan 1987)

sources.citation: McDonough, Joyce. 2003. The prosody of interrogative and focus constructions in Navajo. In A. Carnie, H. Harley & M. Willie (eds.), Formal Approaches to Function in Grammar: In honor of Eloise Jelinek (Linguistik Aktuell 62), 191-206. Amsterdam: Benjamins. [Glottolog id 181704; already_listed]
sources.quote: p.3: "These studies, which are not instrumental studies, report the existence of stress and metrical structure in Northern Athabaskan. McDonough (1990, 1996, 2000a, 2000b) has argued that metrically based structure has no presence in Navajo, and phenomena explained as metrical in Northern Athabaskan are the result of exclusively morphological imperatives in Navajo." p.4: "Navajo has been classified as a tone language with a tone specified for each syllable (Sapir-Hoijer 1967, Young and Morgan 1987)." p.17: "Instrumental studies indicate that the verb stem has many of the properties commonly associated to prominence: longer durations, pitch range expansion, semantic salience"
sources.locator: author preprint pp.3-4 (sec. 1.2-1.3; txt lines 100-104, 139-141), p.16 (sec. 3.2), p.17 (sec. 3.3-4)
sources.note: Instrumental study of yes/no-question and focus intonation; finds no tonal intonation and no focus accent. On word level it states that Navajo has a tone on every syllable, no metrical structure, and that any 'accent' can only fall by default on the rightmost content morpheme, the verb stem, which is phonetically prominent (longer, pitch-range expansion). No word-stress rule; consistent with the catalog's TONAL coding.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1976. Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. handwritten + 30 pp. typescript. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA965L1976b. [Glottolog id 167470, hhtype comparative]
sources.quote: p.9: "In PA there were two suprasegmentals, which in stems were restricted to closed syllables, and could co-occur. They are vowel nasalization (V̨) and what I call vowel constriction (V̓). Vowel constriction is manifest in modern Athabaskan languages as tone." p.11: "In Kutchin, Tanana, Upper Kuskokwim, Sarcee and Navajo as well as other languages not included in this study, the reflex of V̊ [non-constricted] is high tone and the reflex of V̓ [constricted] is low tone. ... In Navajo both *CV̓C, *CvC > CvC; the reflexes of V and V̓ do not contrast in stems having reduced vowels."
sources.locator: typescript p.9 (PDF page 13) and p.11 (PDF page 15); also p.14 (PDF page 18); scanned samples in leer1976_ocr_samples/
sources.note: A comparative-historical paper on how Proto-Athabaskan vowel constriction and stem-final glottalization became tone in the daughter languages; Navajo is one of thirteen languages whose stem-tone reflexes are tabulated (constricted vowel > low tone, non-constricted > high tone; final glottal stop > low tone, p.14). It says nothing about word stress or accent placement in Navajo. Scanned image PDF (86 pp. = annotated draft + clean typescript), no text layer; three typescript pages scanned at 300 dpi, remainder read from contact sheets.
